title: Camels: Built for the Desert
summary: Camels have special bodies for desert life, and they have been important to the people of Arabia for thousands of years.
poll: Camels are still important to life in Saudi Arabia today.

versions.title: Camels: Built for the Desert
versions.text:
Camels live in hot, dry lands. They walk for days on sand. They need just a bit of food. They need just a bit to drink. They are built for the desert.

A camel has a hump. Look at its back. Is the hump full of water? No! It stores fat. It is food for a time of need. Say there is no food. Then the fat gets used. The hump gets small and soft.

Wind blows sand. It stings. But sand stays out of its eyes. It has two rows of long eyelashes. It can shut its nostrils, too.

Its feet are big and wide. They do not sink in the sand. That helps a lot.

A camel can drink a lot at once. It drinks fast. It can drink 100 liters in ten minutes!

Long ago, men rode camels. They went far on the sand. Long lines of camels were called caravans. They took goods and men far. So the camel got a name. It was called the ship of the desert.

Now, we still love them. We drink camel milk. We race them, too. It is a fun sport.

versions.title: Camels: Built for the Desert
versions.text:

The camels of Arabia have one hump. Many people think the hump is full of water. That is not true. The hump stores fat. When food is hard to find, the camel's body slowly burns the fat for energy. As the fat is used up, the hump shrinks. It can even flop over to one side.

Strong desert winds can fill the air with sand. A camel has two rows of long eyelashes. They work like a screen. It can also close its nostrils so sand can't get in.

A camel's feet are wide, with thick, soft pads. When the camel steps, its feet spread out. So it walks on top of the sand and does not sink.

When a camel finds water, it drinks a lot at once. A thirsty camel can drink about 100 liters in ten minutes.

For thousands of years, people in Arabia went on long trips with camels. Long lines of camels were called caravans. They carried goods such as spices and cloth. They also took pilgrims to Makkah. That is why the camel is called "the ship of the desert."

Today, camels still matter a lot. People drink their milk and watch camel races. They go to camel fairs, too.

A camel's feet are broad and cushioned with tough, leathery pads. With every step, they spread across the ground, allowing the camel to walk on top of loose sand rather than sinking into it.

versions.title: Camels: Built for the Desert
versions.text:
Camels are celebrated for their ability to survive in some of the hottest and most arid environments on Earth. They can travel for days across scorching sand with remarkably little food or water, and nearly every feature of a camel's body, from the top of its hump to the soles of its feet, is an adaptation that helps it endure the severe conditions of the desert.

There are two principal species of camel. Dromedaries, which inhabit Arabia and North Africa, have a single hump, whereas Bactrian camels, native to the cold deserts of Central Asia, have two. A widespread misconception holds that a camel's hump is filled with water. In reality, the hump stores fat, a concentrated reserve of nourishment that the animal carries on its back. When food becomes scarce, the camel's body gradually converts this fat into energy, and as the reserve is consumed, the hump shrinks and may even droop to one side until the camel can feed properly again.

Desert sandstorms can fill the air with stinging particles, so the camel possesses several forms of protection. Two rows of long eyelashes shield its eyes, while a thin, transparent third eyelid sweeps away any grains that slip through. A camel can also seal its nostrils tightly, and dense hair inside its ears prevents sand from entering.

A camel's feet are broad and cushioned with tough, leathery pads. With every step, they spread across the ground, distributing the animal's weight so that it walks on top of loose sand rather than sinking into it.

When a camel finally reaches water, it can drink an extraordinary quantity in a short time, approximately 100 liters in roughly ten minutes. Its body is also remarkably efficient at conserving water. A camel's temperature can rise by several degrees during the hottest hours of the day, which reduces how much it needs to sweat.

Camels were domesticated in Arabia about three thousand years ago, and they soon became indispensable partners for the region's people. Long caravans carried trade goods such as spices, textiles, and precious incense across the desert, connecting distant towns and markets. Caravans also transported pilgrims on the long journey to Makkah, which is why the camel earned the nickname "the ship of the desert."

Today, camels remain an essential part of Saudi heritage. Families drink nutritious camel milk, enthusiastic crowds gather for camel races, and major festivals celebrate the animal's beauty and strength.

A widespread misconception holds that a camel's hump is a reservoir of water. In reality, the hump stores fat, a concentrated supply of nourishment the animal carries on its back. Keeping fat in one place, rather than spread beneath the skin, may also help the rest of the body release heat more easily. When vegetation becomes scarce, the camel's body gradually converts this fat into energy, and as the reserve is depleted, the hump shrinks and may even droop to one side until the animal can feed properly again.

Desert sandstorms can saturate the air with stinging particles, so the camel possesses several forms of protection. Two rows of long eyelashes shield its eyes, while a thin, transparent third eyelid sweeps away any grains that slip past them. A camel can also seal its nostrils tightly, and dense hair lining its ears prevents sand from entering.

When a camel finally reaches water, it can consume an extraordinary quantity in a short period, approximately 100 liters in roughly ten minutes. Its body is also exceptionally efficient at conserving that water. A camel's temperature can climb by several degrees during the hottest hours, reducing how much it must sweat, and its kidneys and intestines reclaim so much moisture that its waste is remarkably dry.

Camels were domesticated in Arabia approximately three thousand years ago, and they rapidly became indispensable partners for the region's inhabitants. Extensive caravans transported trade goods such as spices, textiles, and precious incense across the desert, connecting distant settlements and markets. Caravans also conveyed pilgrims on the arduous journey to Makkah, which is why the camel acquired the nickname "the ship of the desert."

Two principal species of camel survive today. Dromedaries, which inhabit Arabia and northern Africa, possess a single hump, whereas Bactrian camels, indigenous to the frigid deserts of Central Asia, have two. A widespread misconception maintains that the hump functions as a reservoir of water. In reality, it stores fat, a concentrated supply of nourishment that the animal transports on its back. Concentrating fat in one location, instead of distributing it beneath the skin, may additionally allow the remainder of the body to release heat more readily. When vegetation becomes scarce, the camel's metabolism gradually converts this fat into energy, and as the reserve is depleted, the hump diminishes and may even collapse to one side until the animal can replenish it.

Desert sandstorms can saturate the atmosphere with abrasive particles, so the camel possesses multiple layers of protection. Two rows of elongated eyelashes shield its eyes, while a thin, transparent third eyelid sweeps away any grains that penetrate this barrier. A camel can also seal its nostrils tightly, and dense hair lining its ears prevents sand from entering.

A camel's feet are broad and cushioned with tough, leathery pads. With every stride, they spread across the surface, distributing the animal's considerable weight so that it travels across loose sand rather than sinking into it.

When a camel finally locates water, it can consume an extraordinary quantity within a brief period, approximately 100 liters in roughly ten minutes. Its physiology is also exceptionally efficient at conserving that moisture. A camel's body temperature can climb by several degrees during the most intense hours of heat, reducing the amount it must sweat, while its kidneys and intestines reclaim so much water that its waste is remarkably dry. Even its oval-shaped blood cells, which differ from the round cells of most mammals, are thought to help keep blood flowing when the animal is dehydrated.

Camels were domesticated in Arabia approximately three thousand years ago, and they rapidly became indispensable partners for the region's inhabitants. Extensive caravans transported commercial goods such as spices, textiles, and precious incense across the desert, connecting distant settlements and marketplaces. Today, camels remain a fundamental element of Saudi heritage. Families consume nutritious camel milk, enthusiastic spectators assemble for camel races, and major festivals celebrate the animal's beauty and endurance. Recognizing this enduring cultural significance, Saudi Arabia designated 2024 as the Year of the Camel.

versions.title: Camels: Built for the Desert
versions.text:
Camels are renowned for their extraordinary capacity to thrive in some of the most inhospitable, arid environments on the entire planet. They can journey for days across scorching dunes with remarkably limited food or water, and virtually every characteristic of a camel's anatomy, from the summit of its hump to the very soles of its feet, represents a specialized evolutionary adaptation that enables it to endure the relentless conditions of desert existence.

When vegetation becomes scarce during prolonged drought, the camel's metabolism progressively converts this fat reserve into usable energy, and as the reserve is gradually depleted, the hump visibly diminishes in size and may even collapse entirely to one side until the animal can replenish it through sustained feeding over subsequent weeks.

Two rows of elongated eyelashes shield its eyes effectively from the worst of the blowing grit, while a thin, transparent third eyelid sweeps away any particles that nonetheless manage to penetrate this initial barrier. A camel can also voluntarily seal its nostrils shut entirely during the height of a storm, and dense hair lining its ears likewise prevents fine sand from infiltrating them.

A camel's feet are broad and heavily cushioned with tough, leathery pads. With every single stride, these feet spread outward across the surface, distributing the animal's considerable body weight so efficiently that it travels across unstable, shifting sand rather than sinking helplessly into it, as most other large animals inevitably would under identical conditions.

questions.why: The article says a camel's big, wide feet spread out, so they do not sink in the sand.

wrong.A: The article does not say speed keeps camels from sinking.
wrong.B: Camels are big, heavy animals; the article says nothing about them being light.
wrong.D: Camels walk across the sand, not only on rock.

questions.stem: "Long lines of camels were called caravans." What is a caravan?
options: A group that travels together
A kind of desert plant
A race for camels on a long track
A tent where camels sleep at night
questions.why: A caravan is a long line of camels and people traveling together across the desert.

wrong.B: The sentence is about lines of camels, not plants.
wrong.C: Races are mentioned later, but a caravan is about traveling, not racing.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article says a caravan is a tent.

questions.stem: A camel has walked for many days with no food. What will its hump most likely look like?
options: Bigger and harder
Full of water
A new color
Smaller and softer
questions.why: The camel uses the fat in its hump when there is no food, so the hump gets smaller and softer.

wrong.A: The hump gets bigger when the camel eats well, not when it has no food.
wrong.B: The hump does not hold water at all.
wrong.C: The article never says the hump changes color.

questions.stem: Why did people call the camel "the ship of the desert"?
options: It first came to Arabia on a big ship.
It carried people and goods across the sand.
Its hump looks a lot like the sail of a ship.
It lived near the sea long ago.
questions.why: Ships carry people and goods across the sea. Camels did the same job across the desert.

wrong.A: The article does not say camels came on ships.
wrong.C: The nickname is about the camel's job, not the shape of its hump.
wrong.D: The article says camels live in the desert, not by the sea.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us that a camel can drink about 100 liters in ten minutes?
options: To show that camels waste water
To explain how camels race
To show a camel can drink a lot at once
To teach how to give a camel water
questions.why: The author uses this fact to show how much water a camel can drink at one time when it finds water.

wrong.A: Drinking a lot at once helps camels; it is not wasting water.
wrong.B: This fact is about drinking, not racing.
wrong.D: The article does not give steps for watering a camel.

LOW.prompt: How does a camel's body help it live in the desert? Use two details from the article.
checklist: I named at least two parts of a camel's body.
I told how each part helps the camel in the desert.
LOW.modelAnswer: A camel's body helps it live in the desert in a few ways. Its hump can store fat, and the camel's body turns this fat into energy when food is hard to find in the desert. A camel can also close its nostrils tightly to keep out blowing sand. Long ago, camels even carried goods for a caravan crossing the desert. These body parts help the camel survive.

keyWords.definition: to stay alive, especially in a hard or dangerous place
keyWords.example: Plants need sunlight and water to survive.

keyWords.definition: the power a body needs to move, work, and grow
keyWords.example: A healthy breakfast gives me energy for the school day.

keyWords.definition: to keep someone or something safe from harm

keyWords.definition: the buying, selling, or swapping of goods between people or places
keyWords.example: The port city grew rich from trade with other countries.

keyWords.definition: very useful, important, or worth a lot
keyWords.example: My grandfather's advice has always been valuable to me.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Camels are the fastest and strongest animals living in any desert.
Camels were useful in the past but not today.
Camels are built for desert life and matter to people in Arabia.
Camels must drink water every single day in order to stay alive.
questions.why: The article explains how the camel's body is suited to the desert and how camels have been important to people in Arabia, past and present.

wrong.A: The article never compares the speed of desert animals.
wrong.B: The last paragraph shows camels are still loved and used today.
wrong.D: The article says camels can travel for days with very little food or water.

questions.stem: How are dromedaries different from the camels of Central Asia?
options: Dromedaries have one hump; the others have two.
Dromedaries live only in the cold deserts of Asia.
Camels of Central Asia have no hump.
Dromedaries cannot drink quickly.

wrong.B: The cold deserts are in Central Asia, where two-humped camels live.
wrong.C: Camels of Central Asia have two humps, not none.
wrong.D: The article says camels of Arabia can drink about 100 liters in about ten minutes.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens to the fat in the hump when food is scarce?
options: It turns into water.
It moves into the camel's legs.
It keeps the camel's skin cool.
The body turns it into energy.

wrong.B: The fat is used up, so the hump shrinks; it does not move to the legs.
wrong.C: The article does not connect the fat to keeping the skin cool.

questions.stem: "When food is scarce, the camel's body slowly turns this fat into energy." What does scarce mean?
options: Fresh
Hard to find
Easy to cook
Too salty
questions.why: When food is scarce, there is very little of it, so it is hard to find. That is why the camel must use its stored fat.

wrong.A: If food were fresh, the camel would not need to use its stored fat.
wrong.C: Camels do not cook food; this meaning does not fit the sentence.
wrong.D: Salt has nothing to do with why the camel uses its fat.

questions.stem: What is the result of a camel's feet spreading out with each step?
options: The camel can run much faster over rocky ground.
It walks on top of soft sand instead of sinking.
Its feet stay cool in the hot sun.
It leaves no footprints behind it in the sand.
questions.why: The article says the wide, padded feet spread out, so the camel walks on top of the sand instead of sinking.

wrong.A: The article talks about sand, not rocks or speed.
wrong.C: The article does not say spreading feet keep them cool.
wrong.D: The article does not mention footprints.

questions.stem: Why were camels "valuable partners" for the people of Arabia?
options: People needed them to cross the desert with goods.
They were sold only for gold and silver coins in markets.
They guarded towns at night.
They were kept only as pets.
questions.why: Camels could cross the desert carrying trade goods and pilgrims, a job that would have been very hard without them.

wrong.B: The article does not say camels were sold for gold.
wrong.C: Nothing in the article says camels guarded towns.
wrong.D: Camels did hard work carrying goods and people, so they were more than pets.

questions.stem: A sandstorm begins. Which features would help a camel MOST?
options: Its wide, padded feet
Its ability to drink quickly
Its fat-filled hump
Its long eyelashes and closing nostrils
questions.why: During a sandstorm, the biggest danger is blowing sand. Long eyelashes, closing nostrils, and ear hair keep sand out.

wrong.A: The feet help with walking on sand, not with blowing sand in the air.
wrong.B: Drinking quickly helps when the camel finds water, not in a storm.
wrong.C: The hump helps when food is scarce, not against sand.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: In time order, from a camel's birth to old age
As a problem with a list of solutions for farmers
Body features first, then camels in history and today
As a comparison between camels and horses
questions.why: The article first describes the camel's hump, eyes, nose, ears, feet, and drinking, and then moves to camels in Arabian history and today.

wrong.A: The article does not follow a camel's life from birth.
wrong.B: The article is not written for farmers or built around one problem.
wrong.D: Horses are not discussed in the article.

MID.prompt: The camel is called "the ship of the desert." Explain why this nickname fits, using one detail about the camel's body and one detail about its history.
checklist: I explained what the nickname means.
I used one detail about the camel's body and one about its history.
I explained how each detail supports the nickname.
MID.modelAnswer: The nickname 'the ship of the desert' fits the camel well because it explains how the animal carries things across the sand the way a ship carries cargo across water. One detail about its body is that the camel's hump stores fat, which its body slowly turns into energy to help it survive when there is little food. One detail about its history is that camels were valuable partners who carried trade goods like spices, cloth, and incense in long caravans across the desert, linking distant towns. Because the camel's body let it survive long desert journeys, it became the perfect way to carry goods and people, which is why people called it a ship of the desert.

keyWords.definition: a body feature or behavior that helps a living thing survive where it lives

keyWords.definition: to use something carefully so that it is not wasted

keyWords.definition: doing a job well without wasting time, energy, or materials

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?

The hump is the only reason the camel survives.
Camel racing is the most important part of Saudi culture.
Desert adaptations made the camel vital to life in Arabia.

wrong.A: The article describes camels as partners, not as animals people struggled to control.
wrong.B: The article describes many adaptations, including eyelashes, nostrils, feet, and water conservation.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does the camel's third eyelid do?

It sweeps away sand that gets past the eyelashes.
It helps the camel see clearly over long distances.
It stores extra water for the eyes.

Sand cannot stick to its fur.

wrong.D: Sand protection comes from eyelashes, nostrils, and ear hair.

questions.stem: "A widespread misconception holds that a camel's hump is filled with water." What does misconception mean?

An old poem
A mistaken idea that many people believe
A rule about animals

wrong.A: A discovery would be true, but this belief is shown to be false.
wrong.B: The sentence describes a belief, not a poem.
wrong.D: The sentence describes a belief, not a rule.

questions.stem: According to the article, about when were camels domesticated in Arabia?

During the twentieth century
After the first cars arrived
About three thousand years ago

wrong.C: Cars are not mentioned, and camels were tamed long before them.

questions.stem: Based on the article, how did camel caravans most likely affect towns in Arabia?
options: They made towns less connected.

They stopped people from traveling to Makkah.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that camels are still part of Saudi heritage?

HIGH.prompt: Choose two of the camel's adaptations and explain how each one solves a problem of desert life. Then explain how these adaptations made camels important in the history of Arabia.
checklist: I explained two adaptations and the problem each one solves.
I connected the adaptations to the camel's role in Arabian history.
I used specific evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Two adaptations that solve real problems of desert life are the camel's hump and its padded feet. The hump is an adaptation that stores fat instead of water, so the camel's body can conserve energy efficiently and slowly convert that fat into fuel when food becomes scarce during a long journey. Its broad, padded feet spread out with every step, solving the problem of sinking into loose sand by letting the camel walk efficiently across the surface instead. Because these adaptations let domesticated camels travel for days with little food or water, they became essential for carrying trade goods and pilgrims across Arabia, which is why the camel remains such an important part of the region's heritage today.
